name: John the Baptist
bio: John's birth was foretold to his father, the priest Zacharias, by the angel Gabriel, who announced that the elderly, childless Zacharias and his wife Elisabeth would have a son who would go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah; Zacharias, struck speechless for doubting, regained his voice only after the child was born and named John as instructed. While Elisabeth was pregnant, her relative Mary, newly pregnant with Jesus, visited her, and the unborn John leaped in the womb at Mary's greeting (Luke 1:5-25, 36-45, 57-80). John the Baptist preached repentance in the Judean wilderness, dressed in camel's hair and living on locusts and wild honey, fulfilling Isaiah's prophecy of a voice crying out to prepare the way of the Lord. Crowds came from Jerusalem and Judea to be baptized by him in the Jordan, confessing their sins; he sharply warned the Pharisees and Sadducees not to presume on their heritage from Abraham, and declared that one far mightier than himself would soon baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire. When Jesus came to be baptized, John objected that he was unworthy, but complied at Jesus's insistence; as Jesus came up from the water, the Spirit descended on him like a dove and a voice from heaven declared him God's beloved Son (Matthew 3:1-17). John's imprisonment, death, and further testimony about Jesus are told in detail in the chapters ahead. When John was imprisoned, Jesus moved from Nazareth to Capernaum and began his public preaching ministry (Matthew 4:12-17). Later, John's own disciples asked Jesus why they fasted while his did not; Jesus replied that his presence was cause for celebration, like a wedding, with fasting to come only after he was taken away (Matthew 9:14-17). From prison, John sent disciples to ask Jesus whether he was truly the Messiah; Jesus pointed to his healings and miracles as the answer. Jesus then praised John to the crowds as more than a prophet, the forerunner foretold by Scripture, greater than anyone born of woman, and identified him as the promised Elijah to come (Matthew 11:2-15). John was imprisoned by Herod the tetrarch (Herod Antipas) for condemning his marriage to Herodias, his brother Philip's former wife. At a banquet, Herodias's daughter danced for Herod, who rashly promised her anything; prompted by her mother, she requested John's head, and Herod reluctantly had him beheaded. His disciples buried his body and told Jesus (Matthew 14:1-12). After his death, some speculated that Jesus might be John risen from the dead (Matthew 16:14). After the Transfiguration, Jesus identified John as the fulfillment of the prophesied return of Elijah (Matthew 17:10-13). When religious leaders questioned Jesus's authority, he turned the question back on them by asking about the source of John's own authority, which they could not answer without political risk (Matthew 21:23-27).
